volumes.title: Casting Off at Ember Mouth
volumes.text:
The ketch Kittiwake left Ember Mouth on the second of September, and I was aboard her. My name is Wren Halloran. I am fourteen, and this journal was a present from my mother, who would rather I had been apprenticed to a draper.

My aunt is Captain Bess Halloran, and she has sailed the Salt Road every autumn for twenty years: north along the Grey Coast, across the open water called the Wide, to the island of Farholm, where the salt pans are. Emberwick cannot cure its fish or its bacon without that salt. We carry wool and candles out, and bring three hundred sacks home.

The crew is Aunt Bess, the mate Mr. Odd, the cook Dunstan, and me, signed on as ship's girl. I waved until the harbour wall was a grey line. Then Mr. Odd handed me a bucket and a scrubbing brush.

volumes.title: The First Night Watch
volumes.text:
Second day out from Ember Mouth, and I have been sick over the lee rail four times. Dunstan the cook says the lee side is the correct side and that I show promise. He gave me ginger tea and told me to watch the horizon, which stays still when nothing else will.

The Kittiwake keeps watches of four hours. Mine is with Mr. Odd, the mate, who is tall, bald and silent as a post. At midnight he woke me by tapping my boot. I stood beside him at the tiller in my aunt's old oilskin while the Grey Coast slid by, a darker dark to larboard.

He showed me the compass in its lit box and how the card swings. He said eleven words in four hours. By the end of it I was no longer sick, and the ship's cat, Biscuit, was asleep in my lap.

volumes.title: Between the Sister Stacks
volumes.text:
Third day on the Salt Road. The Kittiwake came up to the Sister Stacks, seven pillars of black rock standing off the Grey Coast like the stumps of a giant's fence. The tide runs between them fast and pale. Most skippers go round outside and lose half a day.

My aunt, Captain Bess Halloran, goes through the middle, between the third Sister and the fourth. She told me so at breakfast, with a mouth full of porridge.

She took the tiller. Mr. Odd stood in the bows and held up one hand or the other. I was told to sit on the hatch, hold the cat and keep quiet, and I managed two of the three. The rock went by so close I could see the limpets. Then we were out, in flat green water, and Dunstan the cook brought up tea as if nothing had happened.

volumes.title: Fog and the Lead Line
volumes.text:
Fifth day out. We woke inside a cloud. I could not see the bowsprit of the Kittiwake from the tiller. Somewhere to larboard was the Grey Coast, with all its rocks. Nobody could say how far.

So my aunt, Captain Halloran, set me to the lead line. It is a long cord with a lump of lead on the end and bits of leather and rag tied in at each fathom, so you can tell the depth by feel. A hollow in the bottom of the lead is filled with tallow, and brings up a sample of the sea floor.

I called nine fathoms, then eight, then seven. The tallow came up with grey sand, then broken shell. “Shell means the Dunnock bank,” said Mr. Odd, the mate. “We are where we should be.” I have never been so proud of a handful of grit.

volumes.title: Wool for Dunnock Bay
volumes.text:
Sixth day. The fog lifted at noon like a lid, and there was Dunnock Bay half a mile off: a curve of shingle, a stone quay and thirty houses, every one with nets drying on the fence. It is the only harbour on the Salt Road between Ember Mouth and the open sea.

The Kittiwake lay alongside for a day. We landed forty bales of Lowland wool, and I kept the tally while my aunt, Captain Halloran, argued prices with the quay-master. They have argued every September for twenty years. Both enjoy it.

Dunstan the cook took me ashore for fresh bread and a sack of onions. A woman at the bakehouse asked whether I was Bess Halloran's niece, and gave me a currant bun for nothing when I said yes. It seems my aunt is somebody along this coast. She has not mentioned it.

volumes.title: Across the Wide
volumes.text:
Eighth day. North of Dunnock Bay the Grey Coast bends away west and the Salt Road leaves it. Ahead lies the Wide: two days of open water with no land in sight, and the island of Farholm on the far side.

This morning my aunt, Captain Halloran, put me at the tiller of the Kittiwake. Not beside it. At it. “North by east,” she said, “and mind her, she pulls.” Then she went below, or pretended to.

The ketch does pull. She leans on the tiller like a dog on a lead, and the trick is to give a little and take a little and never fight. I held her for an hour, with the compass card steady and my arms shaking. Six dolphins came and rode under the bows. Mr. Odd said they come for good steering. I think that was a joke, his first.

volumes.title: The White Island
volumes.text:
Tenth day out of Ember Mouth. We raised Farholm at dawn, and I thought at first it was snow. The island is low and treeless, and all along its south shore the salt lies heaped in white hills beside the pans.

The pans are shallow ponds floored with clay, hundreds of them, divided by little walls. The tide lets the sea in through a gate. Sun and wind do the rest, all summer, until the water is gone and the salt is left in a crust. The salt-makers rake it up with wooden rakes as broad as a door.

My aunt, Captain Halloran, was met on the jetty by the salt-master, an old man called Imre with a face like a walnut. He looked the Kittiwake over, then me. “Can she carry a sack?” he said. I said I could carry two. That was not true.

volumes.title: Three Hundred Sacks
volumes.text:
Twelfth day. We have been two days loading at Farholm, and I can report that a sack of salt weighs about the same as I do. I carried one, forty times, down a plank into the hold of the Kittiwake, and tonight my shoulders feel as though they belong to somebody else.

Mr. Odd, the mate, stows them. Every sack must sit tight against its neighbour, on boards, clear of the damp. Wet salt is spoiled salt, and three hundred sacks is Emberwick's whole winter. My aunt counts each one into her book. Imre the salt-master counts each one into his. At the end the two books agreed, and they shook hands as though surprised.

Then the salt-makers gave us supper on the shore: flat bread, smoked fish and a soup of seaweed that Dunstan the cook asked the recipe for. I fell asleep sitting up.

volumes.title: Becalmed on the Wide
volumes.text:
Sixteenth day. The Kittiwake left Farholm with three hundred sacks of salt in her and a fair wind. The wind lasted one day. Since then we have lain on the Wide for three days without moving, on a sea like a pewter plate. A piece of orange peel I dropped at breakfast was still alongside at supper.

Nobody is worried except me. My aunt, Captain Halloran, mends a sail. Mr. Odd splices rope and has taught me three knots: the bowline, the clove hitch and the rolling hitch. Dunstan the cook is teaching Biscuit the cat to shake hands.

I asked my aunt how she could bear to sit so still. She said that on the Salt Road you get the weather you are given, and the only thing a sailor can hurry is herself. Then she handed me the other end of the sail.

volumes.title: The Gale and the Pump
volumes.text:
Eighteenth day. The wind we wanted came back, and brought all its relations. By dusk it was blowing a gale from the north-east, and the Kittiwake was running south before it under a scrap of sail, with green water coming over the bows.

My aunt, Captain Halloran, and Mr. Odd took the tiller together. Dunstan the cook and I had the pump. You heave its long iron handle up and down, and the sea you have taken in goes out again in spurts. Three hundred sacks of salt lay under our feet. If the water in the hold reached the boards they sit on, the cargo was lost.

We pumped by turns all night, two hundred strokes each, counting aloud. I was frightened for the first hour. After that I was too tired, and only counted. At dawn the hold was dry and the wind was easing.

volumes.title: The Ember Light
volumes.text:
Twentieth day. After the gale the sea ran in long grey hills, and the Kittiwake climbed each one slowly, heavy with her salt. We had been blown far to the south. Nobody was sure how far. My aunt, Captain Halloran, took a sight of the sun at noon and frowned at her sums.

At dusk she sent me up the mainmast, because I am the lightest. I went up with my heart knocking, hooked an arm round the mast, and looked west.

There was a light. It flashed twice, then stayed dark while I counted ten, then flashed twice again. I shouted it down exactly so. “Two and ten,” my aunt called up. “That is the Ember light. We are a day from home.” Mr. Odd said I had sharp eyes. Dunstan the cook said he had known where we were all along, by the smell.

volumes.title: Salt on the Quay
volumes.text:
Twenty-first day, and the last. The Kittiwake crossed the bar at Ember Mouth on the afternoon flood and came alongside the quay she left three weeks ago. Half of Emberwick seemed to be waiting. The fish-curers had their carts lined up before our ropes were fast.

We swung the salt ashore, three hundred sacks, and my aunt, Captain Halloran, counted them out as carefully as she counted them in. Not one was wet. Mr. Odd allowed himself to look pleased. My mother was on the quay in her good hat, and held me at arm's length to see how brown I was.

Before I went ashore my aunt opened the ship's book. Beside my name she crossed out ship's girl and wrote ordinary seaman, and the date. “The Salt Road goes again next September,” she said. I have nine pages left in this journal. I shall need another.

volumes.title: Outward Bound for Lemons
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, of Ember Mouth. Josiah Marl, master. Day 1. Sailed on the morning tide, wind north-west, fresh. Crew: Mrs. Agnes Tully, mate; Ham Biddle, cook; Pike and Old Sorrel, hands. One hen, named Admiral, for eggs. Our commission is from the Glasshouse Society of Emberwick, who have built a glasshouse and now want something to put in it. We are to sail south to the Lantern Isles and bring home forty young lemon trees, alive. I have carried coal, slates and a church organ. I have never carried an orchard.

Day 3. Wind steady. Made ninety miles by the log line. The last of the Lowlands shore is astern. The Society's secretary supplied a pamphlet on the care of lemon trees. It runs to thirty pages. I have read four. Admiral has laid no egg. The cook says she is settling in.

volumes.title: Fair Wind South
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, bound south for the Lantern Isles to fetch lemon trees. Day 8. Wind north, fair. Ran a hundred and ten miles noon to noon, our best yet. Flying fish seen by Pike, who was not believed until one landed on deck. Ham Biddle fried it. Tasted like herring with ambitions.

Day 9. Warm enough to go without a coat. Mrs. Tully, the mate, has the hands building racks along the deck: forty slots, each to hold a tree in its tub, with a canvas screen to keep off spray. She has read the whole pamphlet. She informs me that lemon trees dislike salt, wind, cold, drought and being moved. I asked what they do like. She said the Lantern Isles.

Day 10. Bread from the Emberwick bakehouse is disappearing faster than five people eat. Suspect rats. Admiral: no egg.

volumes.title: A Stowaway in the Bread
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, southbound for the Lantern Isles. Day 15. The rat has been found. It is four feet six inches high and answers to Tam Reedy, aged eleven, nephew to the baker at Emberwick. He came aboard in the bread locker and has lived since behind the spare sails, on loaves and rainwater. Old Sorrel discovered him by sitting on him.

Day 16. Too far south to turn back. Have entered him in the book as cabin boy, without wages, and written a letter for his aunt to go by the first ship we meet. He says he wished to see a lemon growing. I said most people manage to wish it from the shore.

Day 17. The boy has scrubbed the deck twice unasked and feeds the hen. Admiral laid her first egg, at his feet. The cook is offended.

volumes.title: Flat Calm
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, bound for the Lantern Isles with five crew, one stowaway and a hen. Day 23. No wind. Sea like glass. Made four miles, all of it sideways. Day 24. No wind. Rigged an awning. Mrs. Tully, the mate, set the hands to scraping and painting, on the principle that idle sailors start to sing.

Day 25. No wind. Tam Reedy, the boy, asked whether we were lost. I showed him the chart, the noon sight and my sum, and how the three agree. He asked to try the sum. He got it wrong by two hundred miles, which put us up a mountain. He tried again and got it right. I did not learn it so quickly.

Day 26. A breath from the north-east at sunset. Admiral laid two eggs, the calm suiting her better than it suits me.

volumes.title: Squall and a Sprung Plank
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, bound south for the Lantern Isles. Day 32. Black squall from the west. Shortened sail in time, barely. Rain so thick that Pike, at the bows, could not be seen from the wheel. Caught nine buckets of fresh water off the awning.

Day 33. Ham Biddle, the cook, reports his galley floor wet. A plank has sprung forward, below the waterline. She is taking a bucket an hour. Old Sorrel went into the forepeak with oakum, a mallet and the boy Tam Reedy to hold the lantern, since the boy is the only one who fits.

Day 34. Leak stopped. Sorrel says the boy held the light steady for three hours and did not once complain of the smell. Have amended the book: Reedy, cabin boy, with wages, one penny a day from this date. Admiral: one egg.

volumes.title: The Lantern Isles
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, of Ember Mouth. Josiah Marl, master. Day 41. Landfall. Raised the Lantern Isles, four green hills on the sea with cloud sitting on the tallest. We smelled them before we saw them: warm earth and blossom, after forty days of salt and tar. The boy, Tam Reedy, was at the masthead and nearly fell out of it.

Day 42. Anchored in six fathoms off the town of Marivel, in water so clear the anchor could be seen lying on the sand. The harbour-master asked our business. When I said forty lemon trees for a cold grey town in the north, he laughed for some time, then sent for his cousin.

Day 43. All hands ashore. Lemons grow here in every yard, like apples at home, and nobody looks at them. The boy stood under one for a quarter of an hour.

volumes.title: Forty Trees in Tubs
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, at anchor off Marivel in the Lantern Isles. Day 45. The harbour-master's cousin is a grower, Madam Brin, who has an orchard on the hill. Chose forty lemon trees, three years old, waist high, each in a wooden tub. Price agreed after two hours and a great deal of coffee.

Day 47. She will not release them until we have been taught. All hands attended, the hen excepted. Water at the root, in the evening, fresh and not much. Shade at noon. No salt on the leaf, ever. She made Mrs. Tully, the mate, repeat it. She made me repeat it.

Day 50. Trees carried down by mule and ferried out in the boat, four at a time. All forty stand in their racks on deck. Madam Brin gave the boy, Tam Reedy, a lemon. He will not eat it.

volumes.title: Homeward with an Orchard
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, homeward bound from the Lantern Isles to Ember Mouth. Day 52. Weighed anchor at dawn, wind south-east, light. Forty lemon trees in tubs on deck behind canvas screens. The schooner looks like a hedge under sail.

Day 54. The trees now govern the ship. Screens are shifted with every change of wind. The noon awning goes over the trees first and the helmsman second. Each tree is watered at dusk by Tam Reedy, the cabin boy, one tin mugful each, and he has numbered the tubs in chalk so that none is missed.

Day 56. Spray came aboard on the starboard side. Mrs. Tully, the mate, had all hands up at two in the morning, wiping leaves with fresh water and rags. Never thought to see Old Sorrel dust a tree. Admiral: one egg, laid in tub nineteen.

volumes.title: Short of Water
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, homeward bound for Ember Mouth with lemon trees. Day 60. Head winds for a week. Behind our reckoning, and the fresh water is lower than I like: four casks left, and forty trees drinking beside six people and a hen.

Day 61. Two trees dead, numbers seven and thirty-one, scorched by the salt of five nights ago. Thirty-eight remain. Put all hands on short allowance: three pints a day each. The trees keep their full mug. Ham Biddle, the cook, observed that he had never before been ranked below a shrub. Pike gave half his own water to tree number twelve, thinking himself unobserved.

Day 63. Rain at last, a long soft afternoon of it. Filled two casks. The boy, Tam Reedy, stood in it with his mouth open. Full allowance restored. Admiral: no egg, in protest at the damp.

volumes.title: The Cold Comes Down
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, northbound for Ember Mouth, carrying thirty-eight lemon trees. Day 69. Wind backed north overnight and brought the cold with it. The trees have never met a cold wind in their lives, and showed it by dropping leaves all over my clean deck.

Day 70. Three more dead by morning. Thirty-five remain. Ordered every tub carried below. There are now eleven lemon trees in my cabin, six in the mate's, four in the galley beside the stove, and the rest between decks. I sleep with my feet in foliage. Mrs. Tully says hers rustle.

Day 72. The boy, Tam Reedy, carries a lantern round at night to see that none is in a draught. He has asked whether Emberwick will be too cold for them. I told him about the glasshouse. He had never heard of such a thing.

volumes.title: A Gale in Home Waters
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master, northbound, perhaps eight days from Ember Mouth. Day 79. Glass falling since noon. Sky the colour of slate to the north-west. Doubled the lashings on everything, the lemon trees included.

Day 80. Full gale. Hove to under a storm staysail for fourteen hours, the Heron riding it like the bird she is named for. Below decks, less orderly. A sea struck us on the beam about midnight and the tubs in the galley broke loose. Ham Biddle, the cook, and the boy, Tam Reedy, held them upright with their arms for an hour.

Day 81. Gale blown out. Three trees lost, snapped at the root. Thirty-two remain of the forty. No person hurt, beyond the cook's dignity. Admiral was found in my cabin, roosting in tree number nineteen. She had laid an egg in the tub. I let her stay.

volumes.title: Thirty-Two and a Blossom
volumes.text:
Logbook of the schooner Heron, Josiah Marl, master. Final entries. Day 87. Raised the Grey Coast at dawn. Carried the lemon trees up on deck for the sun, since a ship should come home looking her best. The boy, Tam Reedy, went round with his mug and stopped at tub twelve. One white flower, with a scent that reached the wheel. Pike claims that tree as his own.

Day 88. Crossed the bar at Ember Mouth. The Glasshouse Society was on the quay with a brass band. Landed thirty-two trees of forty, all living, one in blossom. The secretary wept. The baker of Emberwick came aboard, embraced her nephew, and then boxed his ears. Paid off the crew. The boy drew fifty-five pennies and has asked to sign for the next voyage. I have said he must ask his aunt. Admiral goes with the trees. Voyage ends.

volumes.title: Sheet One: Ember Mouth
volumes.text:
Sheet One covers Ember Mouth, from the town quay to the bar, at six inches to the mile. I am Isolde Marrin, surveyor to the Harbour Board of Emberwick, and these are the notes that go with my charts. The Board has asked for the whole Grey Coast, Ember Mouth to Cape Lastlight, in twelve sheets. The last survey is forty years old and marks a sandbank where there is now a fish market.

My vessel is the Plover, a twenty-foot open boat with a brown sail. My assistant is Benno Catt, who is sixteen, rows well and writes a clear figure.

One matter the Board asked me to settle. Two honest skippers have reported a shoal off Gannet Head, the Kettle Shoal, in two different places. A shoal cannot be in two places. I have promised to find where it is, or prove it is nowhere.

volumes.title: Sheet Two: The Marsh Shore
volumes.text:
Sheet Two runs north from Ember Mouth along the marsh shore: six miles of mud, creek and samphire, with no rock bigger than a loaf. It is the easiest sheet to sail and the hardest to draw, because the edge of the land will not stay put. At high water my boat, the Plover, floats over meadows. At low water she sits on mud a mile from the sea.

Benno Catt and I sounded every creek with a marked pole. The marsh people mark the channels with withies, willow sticks pushed into the mud, and move them when the channels move. My note on the chart says: ask at the eel-catcher's hut.

The eel-catcher gave us smoked eel and an opinion. A shoal, he said, is always in one place, and the mistake is always in the man. I wrote that in the margin for Gannet Head.

volumes.title: Sheet Three: The Sister Stacks
volumes.text:
Sheet Three shows the Sister Stacks, seven pillars of black rock a mile off the Grey Coast, and the fast pale water between them. I am Isolde Marrin, surveying for the Harbour Board in the open boat Plover, and I do not mind saying this sheet frightened me.

We could not sound the channels under sail. So Benno Catt rowed, and I swung the lead from the bows, and we worked each gap at slack water, in the twenty minutes when the tide stops to think. Seven Sisters, six channels, nine days. The gap between the third Sister and the fourth carries five fathoms clear. I have marked it, with a warning.

To fix each rock I measured the angle to it from two places on shore. Where the two lines cross on paper, there is the rock. It is the whole of my trade, that crossing of two lines.

volumes.title: Sheet Four: Dunnock Bay
volumes.text:
Sheet Four is Dunnock Bay, the one good harbour between Ember Mouth and Gannet Head: a curve of shingle, a stone quay, and clean sand to anchor in at four fathoms. After the Sister Stacks it was like drawing a teacup.

Benno Catt and I lodged a week above the bakehouse. The church tower makes a fine mark from seaward and I have sketched it in the margin, as it looks from the south-east, so a stranger may know it. A chart should show what a sailor sees, as well as what a bird would.

I asked on the quay about the Kettle Shoal. Everybody knew of it. Nobody had seen it. An old net-mender told me it shows only at the lowest tides of spring, a patch of brown weed and broken water. She pointed north, towards Gannet Head, with her needle.

volumes.title: Sheet Five: The Two Reports
volumes.text:
Sheet Five takes the Grey Coast north from Dunnock Bay to the foot of Gannet Head, eight miles of low cliff. I am Isolde Marrin, surveyor; my boat is the Plover. Here the puzzle of the Kettle Shoal begins, so I set down both reports as the Harbour Board gave them.

Skipper Maddern, fifteen years ago: struck weed and saw rock under his keel, the white house on Gannet Head bearing west-south-west, about a mile off. Skipper Hobb, two years ago: saw broken water close aboard, the white house bearing west-north-west, about a mile off.

The old chart shows one white house on the Head, Hollin Farm. The Board's clerk ruled both bearings from it and marked both places. They lie three-quarters of a mile apart. Benno Catt, my assistant, says one man was mistaken. Both men, I am told, are careful. That is what troubles me.

volumes.title: Sheet Six: Maddern's Mark
volumes.text:
Sheet Six is the south side of Gannet Head, a great grey shoulder of cliff loud with seabirds. Hollin Farm stands on its seaward slope, the white house of the old chart, though forty winters have weathered it nearer to grey.

Here Benno Catt and I went looking for the Kettle Shoal in the first of its two reported places. Skipper Maddern put it a mile off, with the white house bearing west-south-west. I set the Plover on that line and we sounded a square half a mile each way. It took four days.

Fourteen fathoms. Fourteen, fifteen, fourteen. Fine grey sand on the tallow, and never a rock. Whatever Skipper Maddern struck, it is not where the Harbour Board's clerk has drawn it. I wrote on the working sheet: Not here. Benno wanted to add a rude word. I allowed a small one, in pencil.

volumes.title: Sheet Seven: Hobb's Mark
volumes.text:
Sheet Seven covers the water east of Gannet Head, and the second place where the Kettle Shoal is said to lie. Skipper Hobb, two years ago, saw broken water about a mile off, with the white house bearing west-north-west. The Harbour Board's clerk ruled that line from Hollin Farm, the only white house on the old chart.

I am Isolde Marrin, surveyor, and I gave Hobb's mark five days in the open boat Plover. Sixteen fathoms, sand and small shell. A grey seal came up each morning to watch the lead go down. Benno Catt, my assistant, leaned out to see it and went in head first. He came up still holding the pencil.

So neither place is right, and two careful men cannot both have dreamed it. The autumn gales are starting. We run for Pennywell, north of the Head, to winter there and think.

volumes.title: Sheet Eight: Winter at Pennywell
volumes.text:
Sheet Eight is the harbour of Pennywell, three miles north of Gannet Head, where my boat, the Plover, lay under a tarpaulin from November to March. I am Isolde Marrin, surveyor to the Harbour Board. A surveyor's winter is spent indoors, turning pencil soundings into ink. I had a table by the window of the Anchor inn, and Benno Catt ground the ink.

Every evening I laid out the two reports of the Kettle Shoal. Maddern: the white house west-south-west. Hobb: the white house west-north-west. Each says about a mile, but no sailor can judge distance by eye, so I struck that out.

What is left is two lines ruled from one house, spreading apart like the legs of a pair of compasses. Two lines from one point never meet again. Yet both men saw the same shoal. There is my difficulty, drawn plain.

volumes.title: Sheet Nine: Two White Houses
volumes.text:
Sheet Nine is the north side of Gannet Head. In the first week of April, Benno Catt and I took the Plover out of Pennywell and stood south along the cliff, and Benno said, “Which white house is ours, miss?”

There were two. Hollin Farm, far off on the southern slope, weathered almost grey. And much nearer, bright as a tooth, a low cottage that is on no chart at all. We landed and climbed up. It belongs to the Widow Arkle. She limewashed it twelve years ago, she told us, so that her son could find the cove. By my measure it stands a mile and a half north of Hollin Farm.

Twelve years. Maddern made his report fifteen years ago, when Hollin was the only white house and still white. Hobb made his two years ago. I think I know which house Hobb saw.

volumes.title: Sheet Ten: The Kettle Shoal
volumes.text:
Sheet Ten is the smallest of the twelve and gave me the most pleasure. I am Isolde Marrin, surveyor, and this is how the Kettle Shoal was found.

I ruled Skipper Maddern's bearing from Hollin Farm. But I ruled Skipper Hobb's from the Widow Arkle's cottage, a mile and a half away, the white house he truly saw. Two lines from two points. They cross at one place, two miles off Gannet Head: twice as far out as either man guessed.

Benno Catt and I took the Plover there on the lowest tide of April. At the crossing the lead dropped fourteen fathoms, then eight, then stopped at nine feet with weed on it. All round us the water turned brown and began to break. The shoal is two hundred yards long, round, with one spur running out like a spout. Benno cheered. I took forty soundings first.

volumes.title: Sheet Eleven: The Long Strand
volumes.text:
Sheet Eleven carries the Grey Coast north from Pennywell along the Long Strand, fourteen miles of pale sand with dunes behind and nothing on it but terns. I am Isolde Marrin, surveyor to the Harbour Board, in the open boat Plover, with Benno Catt at the oars.

The Strand shelves so gently that a mile out we still had only two fathoms. I have written Shoal water, keep off along the whole length of it. The one mark is a wrecked hull, half buried, which the terns use as a town hall.

We sounded through May with the wind behind us. Benno now takes the angles himself and I check one in five. He has not been wrong since the Sister Stacks. Each evening we could see a little more of the cape ahead, and after dark the light on it, turning.

volumes.title: Sheet Twelve: Cape Lastlight
volumes.text:
Sheet Twelve is Cape Lastlight, where the Grey Coast ends in a spine of rock with a lighthouse on its last knuckle. Beyond it my commission stops. Benno Catt and I sounded round the cape in three calm days of June. The keeper waved from the gallery and lowered us a can of tea on a rope.

In July I laid all twelve sheets on the long table of the Harbour Board in Emberwick. The Kettle Shoal is on Sheet Ten, in one place only, with a note in red: Two white houses on Gannet Head. Be sure which you mean. Skippers Maddern and Hobb both came to look. Each was pleased to learn that he had been right.

A fair copy goes to Emberwick Library. There is a small rock off the Long Strand that had no name. It is now Catt's Tooth. Benno pretends not to mind.

volumes.title: A Hundred and Twelve Steps
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, January. Dear Posy, you asked me to tell you everything, so here is the first of it. Your uncle is now assistant keeper of the Lastlight, at the very end of the Grey Coast. The lighthouse stands on a rock. At low tide you can walk to it from the cape along a causeway of flat stones; at high tide we are an island, and I wave at the mainland like a king.

There are a hundred and twelve steps from the door to the lamp. I have counted them every day for a week, in case one goes missing. At the top is the great lens, taller than I am. It turns and sends one long flash every fifteen seconds.

The senior keeper is Mr. Gant. He has been here nineteen years and has so far said good morning twice. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: Mister Buttons
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, February. Dear Posy, thank you for your drawing of the lighthouse. You have given it a chimney and a cat, neither of which we possess, but I have pinned it up in the lamp room all the same, where the light goes through it every fifteen seconds.

You asked whether I am lonely. Not very. Mr. Gant, the senior keeper, plays draughts with me and wins. And I have made a friend. A grey seal hauls out on the flat rock below the kitchen window each afternoon and lies there like a sack of flour with whiskers. He has two round spots on his chest, so I call him Mister Buttons. I read him your letter. He yawned, but he yawns at everything.

The supply boat comes once a fortnight from Pennywell with oil, flour and the post. Write often. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: Polishing the Glass
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, March. Dear Posy, you want to know what a lighthouse keeper does all day, since the light only shines at night. The answer is that he polishes.

Each morning Mr. Gant and I climb the hundred and twelve steps and draw the curtains round the lens, so the sun cannot shine through it backwards and scorch the place. Then we clean every ring of glass, trim the wicks, fill the oil and wind the clockwork that turns the lens. It has a weight on a chain, like a grandfather clock as tall as a house. My winding arm is getting to be a different shape from the other.

Mr. Gant inspects the glass with his nose an inch off it. Yesterday he found one thumbprint. This morning he said, “That'll do.” I believe that is his highest praise. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: The Fog Bell
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, April. Dear Posy, we have had three days of fog so thick I could not see the sea from the gallery of the lighthouse. In fog a light is no use to anyone. The ships cannot see us, so they must hear us instead.

We have a bell for that, as big as a washtub, hung on the seaward side. A hammer strikes it once every half minute, driven by its own clockwork. For three days and nights it went dong, and we counted thirty, and it went dong. Mr. Gant, the senior keeper, sleeps through it. I have not yet learned how.

On the third evening a fishing boat came creeping past the rock, close in, steering by the sound. A man in the bows lifted his hat to the bell. I lifted mine back, though he could not see me. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: A Tern Called Pin
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, May. Dear Posy, the terns are back, and the lighthouse rock is loud with them. They are white, with black caps and sharp red beaks, and they scold me every time I hang out the washing.

On Tuesday morning I found one on the gallery under the lamp. Birds fly at the light sometimes, and this one had struck the rail and hurt its wing. It could not fly. It could peck, however, and did. I carried it down all hundred and twelve steps in my hat.

It lives in a tea chest in the kitchen now and eats slivers of fish. Mr. Gant, the senior keeper, said a lighthouse was no place for pets, and then spent an hour splinting the wing with a matchstick and thread, very gently. I have named the bird Pin, for the beak. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: Tea on a Rope
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, June. Dear Posy, it hardly gets dark at all now. Mr. Gant and I light the lamp at ten and put it out before four.

We have had visitors. A small open boat with a brown sail spent three calm days sounding the water all round our rock, a lady in the bows swinging a lead line and a boy writing down the numbers. They are making a new chart of the whole Grey Coast. I waved from the gallery and lowered them a can of tea on a rope. So if you ever see the Lastlight on a chart, Posy, your uncle is the dot.

Pin the tern is mending. He walks about the kitchen as if he paid the rent. Mister Buttons the seal has a wife now, or possibly a cousin. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: Pin Flies
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, July. Dear Posy, I have news you will find both sad and glad. Pin, the tern I have nursed in the lighthouse kitchen since May, has flown.

Mr. Gant took the splint off his wing a week ago. Since then we have carried the tea chest out to the foot of the tower and left the lid off. Pin would hop to the edge, stretch both wings, consider the matter and sit down again. I began to think he had decided to be a hen.

Yesterday the wind was light and the other terns were fishing off the causeway. Pin stood on the rim of the chest. Then he simply went, and I lost him among fifty others exactly like him. Mr. Gant said the kitchen would be cleaner. He has not yet moved the tea chest, I notice. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: Counting the Ships
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, August. Dear Posy, you ask whether anything happens at a lighthouse in summer. Everything happens, slowly, a long way off.

We keep a book of every vessel that passes the cape, and this month I am the one who writes it. On Thursday I logged nine fishing boats, two coal brigs, a schooner, and a small yacht with a yellow sail. Each is a line in the book: the hour, the rig, the heading. Mr. Gant, the senior keeper, has nineteen years of such lines on a shelf. He says nobody has ever asked to read them, and that he would be alarmed if they did.

At low tide I walk the causeway to the cape and pick mussels. Mister Buttons the seal follows along in the water beside me, like a dog being taken out. I wish you could see him. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: A Question from Posy
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, September. Dear Posy, your mother writes that you would like to come to the lighthouse at Midwinter, and asks whether it is allowed. I put the question to Mr. Gant, the senior keeper, over the draughts board. He thought for the length of three moves.

Then he said that in nineteen years the Lastlight has had no visitor under the age of forty, that the stairs are steep, the wind is rude and the spare room is full of rope. I took that for a no. Next morning I found him clearing the rope out of the spare room.

So it is settled, if the sea is kind. The supply boat will bring you both from Pennywell on the twentieth of December. Bring your warmest coat and stout boots. The terns have gone south. I looked for Pin among them, but one cannot tell. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: The Night the Clockwork Stopped
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, October. Dear Posy, we have had our first great storm, and I will tell you about it now that it is over and I am dry.

It blew from the north-east for two nights. Spray went clean over the gallery, and the whole tower hummed like a kettle. On the second night, at one in the morning, the clockwork that turns the lens stopped. A link of the chain had jammed. Without it the lamp burns but does not flash, and a ship cannot tell us from any other light on the coast.

So Mr. Gant and I turned the lens by hand. One turned while the other counted fifteen by the watch, turn and turn about, until daylight. He told me the whole history of the lighthouse to keep us awake. It was the most he has ever said. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: Getting Ready
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, November. Dear Posy, three weeks until you come, and the lighthouse has never been so tidy.

Mr. Gant, the senior keeper, has whitewashed the spare room and put up a shelf at a height he judges right for a person of nine. He asked me whether children still liked barley sugar. I said I believed they did. A tin of it arrived on the next supply boat, addressed to nobody.

I have polished the brass rail on all hundred and twelve steps, so mind you do not slip. Your drawings are still pinned round the lamp room, eleven of them now. Mister Buttons the seal is fat for the winter. I have told him to expect company. You shall have a job while you are here, too. I will not say what. It is at the top of the stairs. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.

volumes.title: Posy Lights the Lamp
volumes.text:
Cape Lastlight, the last night of December. Dear Posy, you have been gone three days and the lighthouse is too quiet. Mr. Gant set out the draughts board for three players before he remembered.

I want it written down, so that you can keep it. On Midwinter Eve you climbed a hundred and twelve steps without stopping. You held the long taper, and at a quarter to four you lit the lamp yourself, and every ship on the Grey Coast steered by a light of your making. Mr. Gant entered it in the book: Lamp lit by Posy, visiting keeper. He has written no other visitor's name there in nineteen years.

Mister Buttons misses the herring you threw him. My year here is up tomorrow. I have signed on for another, and your mother says you may come back when the terns do. Your loving uncle, Ambrose.
